claims.text: The isobaric heat capacity of liquid water is notably high compared to most liquids, owing to water's extensive hydrogen-bonding network. At 25 °C, Cp,m ≈ 75.3 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ corresponds to a **specific heat capacity of approximately 4.18 J·g⁻¹·K⁻¹** (dividing by the molar mass of water, 18.015 g/mol). This high heat capacity is a consequence of the energy required to disrupt and reorganize hydrogen bonds as temperature increases, and it is one of the key properties that makes water an exceptional thermal buffer in biological and environmental systems.
claims.reason: Mass conversion and qualitative hydrogen-bond contributions to water thermal buffering are accepted domain knowledge. High specific heatcapacity is not confused here with twice-most-organics molar heatcapacity.

evidence.assessment: Mass conversion and qualitative hydrogen-bond contributions to water thermal buffering are accepted domain knowledge. High specific heatcapacity is not confused here with twice-most-organics molar heatcapacity.

evidence.scope: Background only; never substituted for an original ThermoML measurement.

claims.text: Water's Cp,m passes through a shallow minimum near ~36 °C (~309 K), which is also reflected in the database data — for example, the block from DOI 10.1021/je9002948 shows values rising gently from 75.29 at 303 K to 75.48 at 353 K, consistent with this well-known behavior.
claims.reason: The established shallow35..36C minimum is legitimate background. Original je9002948 has303.15K75.28585512 and353.15K75.4840232 at 101.325 kPa; the series endpoints are correct and broadly consistent, though not independent proof of the exact minimum.

evidence.assessment: The established shallow35..36C minimum is legitimate background. Original je9002948 has303.15K75.28585512 and353.15K75.4840232 at 101.325 kPa; the series endpoints are correct and broadly consistent, though not independent proof of the exact minimum.
